newsitem.title: UGANDA: Uganda announces major currency, trade reforms.
newsitem.headline: Uganda announces major currency, trade reforms.

text.p: Uganda on Thursday made sweeping reforms in currency and trade regulations, including allowing imports of beer, batteries and soft drinks banned several years ago to boost local manufacturing.

Capital accounts will be liberalised to complete reforms in the foreign currency regime and reinforce confidence in the government's commitment to prudent fiscal and monetary policies, Finance Minister Jehoash Mayanja-Nkangi said.

"The change means that residents and non-residents will be free to bring in and take out capital without restriction. Residents will be free to hold foreign accounts and instruments outside the country. Non-residents will be able to hold foreign exchange accounts in the domestic banking system and instruments denominated in Ugandan shillings," he added.

Proposals to repeal the Exchange Control Act and legislation regarding money laundering will be presented to parliament in July, he said when he presented his 1997/98 budget proposals to the Ugandan parliament in the capital.
The reform also means Ugandans are free to hold and use foreign credit cards as long as they are creditworthy.

In April 1998, the bans on the import of beer, sodas and batteries will be terminated. In April 1999, the ban on cigarette imports will be lifted. The bans will be replaced with surcharges that will be phased out within three years.

The minister reduced all import duty rates to 20 from 30 percent and said he had harmonised excise duty applicable to imports to 10 percent. The overall import duty will be further reduced to 15 percent in 1998/99 and thereafter to 7.0 percent.
The 10 percent excise duty will be abolished after 1998/99 when the government will establish a new low uniform duty.
The duty changes affected countries outside the 23-member Common Market for Southern and Eastern Africa (COMESA) since COMESA countries had their own tariff arrangements, he said.
